source_text: –Ἀλλὰ τί χρήσῃ τῷ πλούτῳ; Ἐσθῆτι πολυτιμήτῳ περιβαλεῖς σεαυτόν; Οὐκοῦν δύο μέν σοι πηχῶν χιτωνίσκος ἀρκέσει, ἑνὸς δὲ ἱματίου περιβολὴ πᾶσαν τῶν ἐνδυμάτων ἐκπληρώσει τὴν χρείαν. Ἀλλ' εἰς τροφὴν καταχρήσῃ τῷ πλούτῳ; Εἷς ἄρτος ἱκανὸς ἀποπληρῶσαι γαστέρα. Τί οὖν λυπῇ; ὡς τίνος στερούμενος; δόξης τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ πλούτου; Ἀλλ' ἐὰν μὴ χαμαὶ ζητήσῃς τὴν δόξαν, εὑρήσεις τὴν ἀληθινὴν ἐκείνην καὶ λαμπρὰν προάγουσάν σε ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν. Ἀλλ' αὐτὸ τὸ ἔχειν τὸν πλοῦτον ἀγαπητόν ἐστι, κἂν μηδὲν ἀπ' αὐτοῦ περιγίνεται ὄφελος. Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἀνόνητός ἐστιν ἡ τῶν ἀχρήστων σπουδὴ, παντὶ γνώριμον. Πλὴν ἀλλὰ παράδοξον ἴσως φανεῖταί σοι ὃ μέλλω λέγειν· παντὸς δέ ἐστιν ἀληθέστερον. Σκορπιζόμενος ὁ πλοῦτος, καθ' ὃν ὁ Κύριος ὑποτίθεται τρόπον, πέφυκε παραμένειν· συνεχόμενος δὲ, ἀλλοτριοῦσθαι. Ἐὰν φυλάσ σῃς, οὐκ ἔχεις· ἐὰν σκορπίσῃς, οὐκ ἀπολεῖς· Ἐσκόρπισε γὰρ, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν· ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα· Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ ἱματίων ἕνεκεν οὐδὲ τροφῶν ὁ πλοῦτός ἐστι τοῖς πολλοῖς περισπούδαστος, ἀλλά τις ἐπινενόηται μεθοδεία τῷ διαβόλῳ, μυρίας τοῖς πλουσίοις δαπάνης ἀφορμὰς ὑποβάλλουσα, ὥστε τὰ περιττὰ καὶ ἄχρηστα ὡς ἀναγκαῖα σπου δάζεσθαι, μηδὲν δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐξαρκεῖν πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀναλωμάτων ἐπίνοιαν. Καταμερίζουσι γὰρ τὸν πλοῦτον πρός τε τὴν παροῦσαν χρείαν, καὶ πρὸς τὴν μέλλουσαν· καὶ τὸν μὲν ἑαυτοῖς, τὸν δὲ παισὶν ἀποτίθενται. Εἶτα καὶ διαιροῦσι τὸν αὐτὸν εἰς ἀφορμὰς δαπάνης ποικίλης. Οἷαι γὰρ αὐτῶν αἱ διατάξεις, ἄκουσον. Ἔστω, φησὶν, ὁ μὲν ἐν χρήσει πλοῦτος, ὁ δὲ ἀπό θετος· καὶ ὁ ταῖς χρείαις ὑπηρετούμενος ὑπερβαινέτω τῶν ἀναγκαίων τὸν ὅρον· οὗτος πρὸς τὰς κατ' οἶκον πολυτελείας παρέστω, ἐκεῖνος πρὸς τὰς ἔξωθεν φαντασίας ὑπηρετείτω· ὁ μὲν ὁδοιποροῦντι χορηγείτω τὴν πολυτέλειαν, ὁ δὲ ἐφ' ἑστίας μένοντι λαμπρὸν καὶ περίβλεπτον κατασκευαζέτω τὸν βίον· ὥστε μοι θαυμάζειν ἔπεισι τῶν περιττῶν τὴν ἐπίνοιαν. Ὀχήματά ἐστι μυρία, τὰ μὲν σκευαγωγοῦντα, τὰ δὲ αὐτοὺς περιφέροντα, χαλκῷ καὶ ἀργύρῳ κεκαλυμμένα. Ἵπποι παμπληθεῖς, καὶ οὗτοι γενεαλογού μενοι ἀπὸ εὐγενείας πατέρων, ὥσπερ οἱ ἄνθρωποι. Οἱ μὲν τρυφῶντας αὐτοὺς κατὰ τὴν πόλιν περιφέρουσιν· ἄλλοι συνθηρεύουσιν, ἄλλοι πρὸς ὁδοιπορίαν ἐξησκημένοι. Χαλινοὶ καὶ ζῶναι καὶ περιδέῤῥεα, πάντα ἀργυρᾶ, πάντα χρυσόπαστα. Τάπητες ἁλουργοὶ, κοσμοῦντες τοὺς ἵππους ὥσπερ νυμφίους· ἡμιόνων πλῆθος, κατὰ χρόαν διῃρημένων· ἡνίοχοι τούτων, ἀλλήλων διάδοχοι, οἱ προτρέχοντες, οἱ παρεπόμενοι. Τῶν ἄλλων οἰκετῶν ἀριθμὸς ἄπειρος πρὸς πᾶσαν αὐτοῖς πολυτέλειαν ἐξαρκῶν· ἐπίτροποι, ταμίαι, γεωργοὶ, παντοδαπῆς ἔμπειροι τέχνης, τῆς τε ἀναγκαίας καὶ τῆς πρὸς ἀπόλαυσιν καὶ τρυφὴν εὑρημένης· μάγειροι, σιτοποιοὶ, οἰνοχόοι, θηρευταὶ, πλάσται, ζωγράφοι, ἡδονῆς παντοίας δημιουργοί. Ἀγέλαι καμ ήλων, τῶν μὲν ἀχθοφόρων, τῶν δὲ νομάδων, ἵππων ἀγέλαι, βουκόλια, ποίμνια, συφόρβια, οἱ τούτων νομεῖς, γῆ ἡ πᾶσι τούτοις πρὸς τροφὴν ἐξαρκοῦσα, καὶ ἔτι ταῖς προσόδοις τὸν πλοῦτον αὔξουσα· λουτρὰ ἐν πόλει· λου τρὰ κατ' ἀγρούς· οἶκοι παντοδαποῖς μαρμάροις περιλαμπόμενοι, ὁ μὲν Φρυγίου λίθου, ἄλλος Λακωνικῆς ἢ Θεσσαλικῆς πλακός· καὶ τούτων οἱ μὲν ἐν χειμῶνι θάλποντες, οἱ δὲ ἀναψύχοντες ἐν τῷ θέρει. Ἔδαφος ταῖς ψηφῖσι διηνθισμένον, χρυσὸς ὑπαλείφων τὸν ὄροφον. Ὅσον δὲ τῶν τοίχων διαφεύγει τὴν πλάκα, τοῖς τῆς γραφικῆς ἄνθεσι καλλωπίζεται.
thought_title: The uselessness and restless multiplication of wealth
orientation: Basil continues addressing the rich directly, arguing that wealth cannot satisfy even the body's small needs and that hoarded wealth is lost while scattered wealth endures.
pass_a_gloss: But what will you do with the wealth? Will you clothe yourself with costly clothing? Well then, a tunic of two cubits will suffice for you, and the wrapping of one cloak will fulfill the whole need of garments. But will you use up the wealth for food? One loaf is sufficient to fill the belly. Why then do you grieve? As being deprived of what? Of the glory that comes from wealth? But if you do not seek glory on the ground, you will find that true and bright glory going before you in the kingdom of heaven. But the very having of wealth is loved, even if no benefit comes from it. That the zeal for useless things is unprofitable is known to everyone. But yet perhaps what I am about to say will seem paradoxical to you; but it is truer than everything. Wealth being scattered, according to the manner which the Lord prescribes, is by nature able to remain; but being held together, to be alienated. If you guard it, you do not have it; if you scatter it, you will not lose it. For he scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever. But not for the sake of garments nor of foods is wealth eagerly desired by the many, but some scheme has been devised by the devil, suggesting to the rich countless occasions of expense, so that the superfluous and useless things are eagerly pursued as necessary, and nothing is sufficient for them for the devising of expenditures. For they divide up the wealth for the present need and for the future; and they store away some for themselves, and some for their children. Then they also divide the same wealth into occasions of varied expense. For what their arrangements are like, listen. Let it be, he says, that one part of the wealth is in use, and the other is stored away; and let the wealth serving the needs exceed the boundary of what is necessary; let this one be present for the extravagances in the house, let that one serve for the outward displays; let one supply extravagance for the one traveling, let the other make the life of the one staying at home brilliant and conspicuous; so that I am moved to marvel at the devising of superfluous things. There are countless vehicles, some carrying baggage, others carrying them around, covered with bronze and silver. Horses in great abundance, and these being traced in lineage from nobility of fathers, just like humans. Some carry them around the city living in luxury; others hunt with them; others are trained for travel. Bridles and belts and breastplates, all silver, all gold-spangled. Purple carpets, adorning the horses like bridegrooms; a multitude of mules, divided according to color; their drivers, succeeding one another, those running ahead, those following alongside. The number of the other household slaves is boundless, sufficient for every extravagance for them; overseers, stewards, farmers, experienced in every kind of craft, both the necessary and the one invented for enjoyment and luxury; cooks, bakers, cupbearers, hunters, modelers, painters, craftsmen of every kind of pleasure. Herds of camels, some burden-bearing, some grazing; herds of horses, herds of cattle, flocks, swineherds, their herdsmen; land sufficient for food for all these, and still increasing the wealth with its revenues; baths in the city; baths in the country; houses shining all around with all kinds of marbles, one of Phrygian stone, another of Laconian or Thessalian slab; and of these some warming in winter, others cooling in summer. Floor adorned with mosaic stones, gold overlaying the roof. And as much of the walls as escapes the slab is beautified with the flowers of painting.

choices.why: Glossary term; 'wealth' is required and fits the argument about surplus possessions.
Keeps the literal force of the participle and echoes the Psalm quotation 'he scattered'; 'scattered' is the biblical idiom for generous giving.
Literal rendering of the passive participle; Basil contrasts scattering with holding wealth together, i.e., hoarding.
Preserves the passive infinitive and the sense of wealth becoming foreign or lost to its holder.
Renders the devil's cunning device; 'scheme' captures the deliberate, deceptive planning.
The word means starting points or pretexts for expense; 'occasions' keeps the sense of opportunities the devil suggests.

bible_refs.note: Ἐσκόρπισε γὰρ, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν· ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα

pass_b_english: “But what will you do with your wealth? Will you wrap yourself in costly clothing? A little tunic of two cubits will be enough for you, and the covering of a single cloak will fulfill the entire need for garments. Will you use your wealth for food? One loaf is enough to fill a stomach. Why then do you grieve? As one deprived of what? Of the glory that comes from wealth? But if you do not seek glory on the ground, you will find that true and radiant glory going before you in the kingdom of heaven. But the very having of wealth is lovable, even if no benefit comes from it.” That the zeal for useless things is unprofitable is known to everyone. Yet what I am about to say will perhaps seem strange to you, but it is truer than anything. Wealth, when scattered in the way the Lord prescribes, naturally remains; when held together, it is alienated. If you guard it, you do not have it; if you scatter it, you will not lose it. For he scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever (Psalm 112:9, LXX 111:9). But wealth is not eagerly sought by most people for the sake of clothing or food. Rather, the devil has devised a scheme that suggests to the rich a thousand occasions for expense, so that what is superfluous and useless is pursued as necessary, and nothing is ever enough for them in their devising of expenditures. For they divide their wealth between present need and future need, and they set aside one portion for themselves and another for their children. Then they divide the same wealth again into occasions for varied spending. Listen to what their arrangements are like. “Let one part of the wealth be in use,” he says, “and another in reserve. Let the part that serves needs go beyond the limit of what is necessary: let this one be ready for the extravagances of the household, and let that one serve for outward display. Let one supply extravagance for the traveler, and let the other make the life of the one who stays at home brilliant and admired.” So I am moved to marvel at the devising of superfluities. There are countless vehicles, some carrying baggage, others carrying the rich themselves, covered with bronze and silver. There are horses in great abundance, and these are traced in lineage from noble fathers, just like human beings. Some carry the rich as they live luxuriously through the city; others join in the hunt; others are trained for travel. Bridles and belts and collars, all silver, all inlaid with gold. Purple-dyed tapestries adorn the horses like bridegrooms. There is a multitude of mules, divided by color; their drivers succeed one another, some running ahead, some following alongside. Of the other household servants the number is boundless, sufficient for every extravagance: stewards, treasurers, farmers, skilled in every kind of craft, both the necessary and the one invented for enjoyment and luxury; cooks, bakers, cupbearers, hunters, sculptors, painters, craftsmen of every kind of pleasure. There are herds of camels, some for carrying burdens, some for pasturage; herds of horses, herds of cattle, flocks of sheep, herds of swine, and their keepers; land sufficient to feed all these, and still increasing the wealth by its revenues; baths in the city; baths in the country; houses gleaming with all kinds of marble, one with Phrygian stone, another with Laconian or Thessalian slabs; and of these, some warming in winter, others cooling in summer. The floor is adorned with mosaic stones, gold overlays the roof. And as much of the walls as escapes the stone facing is beautified with the flowers of painting.

problems.why: νομάδων means 'grazing' or 'pasturing', but in context of camels, this means 'grazing camels' or 'pastured camels' as opposed to burden-bearing ones; but 'for grazing' is ambiguous—it could mean the camels graze or are for being grazed upon.
περιδέρραια (or περιδέραια) means 'necklaces/collars' or 'ornaments for the neck/shoulders of horses', not 'breastplates' which is a different piece of armor (θώραξ).
problems.ruling: περιδέῤῥεα = neck ornaments/collars, not 'breastplates' (θώραξ). Wrong item, misleading.

fixed: Changed 'some for grazing' to 'some for pasturage' to clarify that the camels are pastured, not grazed upon.
Changed 'breastplates' to 'collars' because περιδέῤῥεα refers to neck ornaments, not armor.

last_rejected.why: Vehicles 'covered with bronze and silver' implies metal-plated; context of luxury suggests inlaid or overlaid decoration, not fully covered.
last_rejected.ruling: 'κεκαλυμμένα' = covered/concealed; 'covered with bronze and silver' is within normal range; 'inlaid' would be interpretive preference.

last_rejected.quote: A little tunic of two cubits
last_rejected.why: πηχῶν is genitive plural, 'of two cubits' describes length, not 'a little tunic of two cubits' which misrepresents the measurement as modifying 'little'
last_rejected.fix: A tunic of two cubits will be enough for you
last_rejected.ruling: δυο πηχων χιτωνισκος naturally reads 'tunic of two cubits'; English conveys the measurement correctly.

last_rejected.quote: the covering of a single cloak
last_rejected.why: ἱματίου is 'cloak/outer garment,' but 'covering of a single cloak' is tautological; περιβολὴ means 'wrapping/wearing' or 'covering,' but the sense is 'the wearing of one cloak'
last_rejected.fix: and one cloak will fulfill every need for garments
last_rejected.ruling: περιβολή means 'covering/wrapping'; 'covering of a single cloak' accurately renders ἑνός ἱματίου περιβολή without real error.

last_rejected.quote: That the zeal for useless things is unprofitable
last_rejected.source_quote: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἀνόνητός ἐστιν ἡ τῶν ἀχρήστων σπουδή
last_rejected.why: σπουδή is 'eagerness/diligence/effort,' not 'zeal'; 'zeal' is too strong and religiously connoted. The sense is 'eagerness for useless things'
last_rejected.fix: That eagerness for useless things is unprofitable
last_rejected.ruling: σπουδή includes 'zeal' within its range; not a major meaning change, merely a preference.

last_rejected.why: πέφυκε means 'is by nature disposed to' or 'naturally tends to,' but 'naturally remains' loses the sense of inherent tendency; more importantly, the contrast is between scattered wealth that 'stays with you' vs. held wealth that 'is alienated'
last_rejected.ruling: πέφυκε παραμένειν = 'naturally remains'; captures the inherent tendency. Contrast with ἀλλοτιοῦσθαι is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: when held together, it is alienated
last_rejected.why: συνεχόμενος is passive 'when held together/restrained,' but 'alienated' is ambiguous; ἀλλοτριοῦσθαι means 'becomes another's/is estranged/is lost to you.' The point is hoarded wealth becomes someone else's
last_rejected.fix: when held together, it becomes another's
last_rejected.ruling: ἀλλοτιοῦσθαι = 'alienated/estranged'; standard rendering. The point that hoarded wealth is lost is conveyed.

last_rejected.quote: If you guard it, you do not have it
last_rejected.why: Correct translation, but the following 'if you scatter it, you will not lose it' misses the paradox: guarding = not having, scattering = not losing. The English is accurate here.
last_rejected.ruling: The reporter confirms the English is accurate; no error exists here.

last_rejected.quote: For he scattered, he gave to the poor
last_rejected.why: The subject is unclear; this quotes Psalm 112:9 (LXX 111:9) about the righteous man. 'He' could mislead. The Greek has no expressed subject, but the psalm speaks of the righteous man. However, this is a minor issue.
last_rejected.fix: For he has scattered, he has given to the poor
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter calls this minor; 'he' for the righteous man in a psalm quote is standard and not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: suggests to the rich a thousand occasions for expense
last_rejected.source_quote: μυρίας τοῖς πλουσίοις δαπάνης ἀφορμὰς ὑποβάλλουσα
last_rejected.why: ὑποβάλλουσα is 'suggesting/putting into their minds,' but 'occasions for expense' misses that ἀφορμάς means 'starting-points/opportunities/pretexts' — the devil supplies pretexts for spending
last_rejected.fix: suggesting to the rich countless pretexts for spending
last_rejected.ruling: ἀφορμάς means 'occasions/opportunities'; 'occasions for expense' is within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Let the part that serves needs go beyond the limit of what is necessary
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ ταῖς χρείαις ὑπηρετούμενος ὑπερβαινέτω τῶν ἀναγκαίων τὸν ὅρον
last_rejected.why: This is the rich man's voice/arrangement, but 'let...go beyond' makes it sound like Basil's advice. The Greek is jussive 'let it exceed' as part of the rich man's scheme, but the English could mislead. More importantly, this is the rich man's sinful plan, not advice.
last_rejected.fix: let the part serving needs exceed the limit of necessities
last_rejected.ruling: Jussive 'let it exceed' is in the rich man's quoted speech (φησί); context prevents misreading as Basil's advice.
